summary: This document updates RFC 7643 and RFC 7644 with new SCIM query parameters and result attributes for cursor-based pagination. It helps SCIM services built on systems that already page through results with cursors rather than numeric offsets.

eli5.summary: When reading a long book, a bookmark is better than counting pages. This lets SCIM servers hand out bookmarks to continue through a long list of users.

subtitle: Bookmark-style paging for SCIM, so servers built on cursors need not translate to page numbers.

tldr.problem: SCIM only offered index-based pagination, so a service provider built on a cursor-based system had to iterate the whole cursor, store the results and serve indexed pages from them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9865 adds a cursor query parameter and nextCursor and previousCursor response attributes, new error types, and a pagination block in ServiceProviderConfig so clients can discover what is supported.
tldr.outcome: SCIM servers can reuse their existing cursors directly, and clients walk through results by passing back the opaque cursor each response gives them.

today: RFC 9865 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It updates RFC 7643 and RFC 7644, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Cursors for SCIM
sections.content:
The two common patterns for paging through results are index-based and cursor-based. The RFC does not compare them. It observes that SCIM service providers usually sit on top of existing codebases, databases or APIs that already have an established pagination pattern.

Translating an underlying cursor into the index-based pagination of RFC 7644 requires the provider to fully iterate the cursor, store the results, and then serve indexed pages from them. This pagination translation adds complexity and memory requirements, and may impede SCIM adoption.

The RFC adds a simple extension that lets providers reuse cursors. It updates RFC 7643 and RFC 7644 because it adds attributes to their existing structures; the changes apply when the cursor parameter is used in GET or POST search requests.
sections.eli5: Counting to page 57 means flipping through every page before it. A bookmark lets you open the book right where you stopped.

sections.title: Cursor Parameters and Responses
sections.content:
A client sends two query parameters. cursor is the nextCursor value from a previous page; it MUST be empty or omitted on the first request and may only contain unreserved characters from RFC 3986. count is the desired maximum number of results per page; a negative value is read as 0, and 0 means return no resources except totalResults. The provider MUST NOT return more than count, though it MAY return fewer.

Responses carry nextCursor, which providers MUST include in every paged response except the last page, and an optional previousCursor, which MUST NOT appear on the first page. Cursors are URL-safe strings that are opaque to the client. To fetch another page, the client repeats the query with every parameter identical except the cursor, which SHOULD be a value the provider returned earlier.

Providers that cannot estimate totalResults MAY omit it. If sorting is implemented, cursor-paged results should be sorted.
sections.eli5: The server gives you a ticket after each page. You hand the ticket back to get the next page, and you never need to read what is on the ticket.

sections.title: Pagination Errors
sections.content:
For invalid cursor or count values and other error conditions, a provider SHOULD return the appropriate HTTP status code and a JSON error as defined in RFC 7644. For status 400 (Bad Request), three new scimType values are added: invalidCursor, expiredCursor and invalidCount.

An expired cursor means the client waited longer than the provider's cursorTimeout. An invalid count must be between 0 and the provider's maxPageSize and must equal the count of the initial query.
sections.eli5: If you lose your ticket, or wait so long that it stops working, the server tells you which of those went wrong.

sections.title: Choosing Cursor, Index or Both
sections.content:
A provider MAY require cursors for all results by including a nextCursor even when the query had no cursor parameter. In the RFC's example, a plain GET /Users returns a page of defaultPageSize results (100 of 5000 total) and a nextCursor.

A provider supporting both methods lets clients pick with startIndex or cursor, and MUST choose a default method for requests that specify neither. Providers that previously supported only index pagination should keep index as the default, to avoid breaking clients that expect it.

Queries can also be sent with HTTP POST to /.search, passing cursor and count in the request body.
sections.eli5: A library that adds bookmarks should still let old visitors count pages, so nothing breaks for them.

sections.title: Discovering Support
sections.content:
A provider implementing cursors SHOULD add an optional pagination complex attribute to its /ServiceProviderConfig document. Its sub-attributes are cursor and index (REQUIRED Booleans), and the OPTIONAL defaultPaginationMethod (cursor or index), defaultPageSize, maxPageSize and cursorTimeout (the minimum number of seconds a cursor stays valid between page requests).

A client MAY fetch this document before using cursors. Clients MUST NOT treat missing values as meaning there are no defaults, limits or cursor lifetimes; a provider may leave them out because, for example, different resource types have different values, or because page size depends on the size of each resource.
sections.eli5: Before borrowing a bookmark, you can ask the library desk what rules it uses, though it may not tell you every rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names two threats: malicious actors, authenticated or not, who try to read or change data through cursor queries or to exhaust resources, and benign authenticated users who accidentally overload the provider.

For confidentiality, paging MUST stay confined to what the current identity may access, even if the actor holds a cursor made by someone else. Authorization checks MUST continue as the actor moves through results, and holding a cursor must never grant extra access. Providers SHOULD invalidate an actor's cursors after a permission change when possible, should obfuscate cursors so they cannot be forged, and MUST NOT leak sensitive data in error messages.

For availability, storing much state per cursor could let many initial queries exhaust resources. Recommended defenses include requiring authentication for large result sets (anonymous queries may get a 400 with tooMany), rate limiting as in RFC 6585, administrator limits on cursors or maxPageSize, and resource-efficient cursor invalidation.
sections.eli5: A bookmark must not let you read pages you are not allowed to see, and the library must not run out of bookmarks if someone grabs thousands.

viz.caption: CURSOR PAGING EXCHANGE (BASED ON THE RFC'S EXAMPLE)

messages.label: GET /Users?...&cursor&count=10
messages.note: Empty cursor requests the first page.

messages.label: 200 OK with nextCursor
messages.note: Page of up to 10 resources plus a cursor for the next page.

messages.label: GET ... cursor=(nextCursor)&count=10
messages.note: Same parameters; only the cursor changes.

messages.label: 200 OK with previousCursor and nextCursor
messages.note: nextCursor is omitted on the last page.

items.label: Invalid cursor
items.desc: Cursor should be empty for page one, then a nextCursor or previousCursor value.

items.label: Expired cursor
items.desc: The client waited longer than the provider's cursorTimeout.

items.label: Invalid count
items.desc: Must be between 0 and maxPageSize and equal the initial query's count.
